title: The Best AI Ideas Start in Your Most Boring Chores
summary: Useful AI ideas come from the chores you repeat every week. How to split work into reading and deciding, test the jagged frontier and pilot with a human gate.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Monday, 9:40. A new hire asks for the onboarding doc link, again. Someone on support scrolls through three help articles looking for the one paragraph about refunds on annual plans. Finance has a bank statement in one window and the ledger in the other and matches rows by eye. Your lead spends twenty minutes before a partner call rereading old email threads. Nobody would call any of this a problem. It's just Monday.

That list is where most useful AI ideas start. Big demos are fun to watch, but the ideas that stick usually come from someone noticing a small chore they do every week and asking whether a model could take the first pass. This post is about getting good at that noticing, then testing an idea without betting the team on it.

Split each chore into reading and deciding

Take any repetitive task and pull it apart. Some steps are reading, gathering, matching, reformatting, drafting and sorting. Others are decisions: is this refund allowed, is this candidate a fit, does this transaction look off. Language models handle a lot of the first kind well. The second kind needs your team's judgment, context and someone who answers for the result.

Once you look at work this way, ideas turn up everywhere:

  • The onboarding PDF nobody reads becomes a short path for each new hire. The model pulls the sections that matter for their role and writes a few check questions. Their buddy still answers the real questions.
  • The support knowledge that lives in two people's heads becomes searchable, and agents get a drafted reply with a link to the source article. The agent still decides what to send.
  • Bank reconciliation gets a first pass that pairs matching rows and flags the leftovers. A person still signs off on every mismatch.
  • Meeting prep becomes a one-page brief built from the last few threads and notes. You still decide what to push for on the call.

Same pattern every time: AI takes the reading and the drafting, a person keeps the call. It's also the cheapest way to start, because nobody has to trust the model with a decision on day one.

Check which side of the frontier the task sits on

Here's the catch. Two tasks that feel equally hard to you can be very different for a model. In 2023, researchers from Harvard Business School, Wharton, MIT Sloan and Boston Consulting Group ran a field experiment with 758 BCG consultants (Dell'Acqua et al., 2023). On 18 realistic consulting tasks that GPT-4 handled well, consultants using it completed 12.2% more tasks, worked 25.1% faster and produced work rated more than 40% higher in quality than a control group. On one task picked to sit outside what the model could do, consultants with AI were 19 percentage points less likely to reach a correct answer than those working without it.

The authors call this a "jagged technological frontier". The edge isn't where you'd guess, and a fluent answer reads the same on both sides of it. So before you build anything, run the chore through a model a handful of times with real inputs and compare the output against answers you already know are right. If it stumbles on the cases that matter, you just learned something for the price of an afternoon.

A second study hints at who gains the most. Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond followed 5,179 customer support agents who got an AI assistant that suggested replies (Generative AI at Work, NBER). Issues resolved per hour rose 14% on average and 34% for novice and low-skilled agents, with minimal impact on experienced, highly skilled ones. The authors call it suggestive evidence that the tool passed on the habits of the strongest agents to everyone else. That's a good reason to look at onboarding and support early.

Two studies, two settings

Both studies used 2023-era models in specific jobs: consulting tasks at BCG and chat support at one company. Newer models have moved the frontier since then (checked November 2026). Use the numbers as a reason to test inside your own work, and skip the slide that promises your team a 40% boost.

Where it gets hard

A demo that answers questions takes an afternoon. A workflow your team relies on takes more: data clean enough to use, clear access rules, a step where a person reviews the output, a record of who decided what, and a short list of things the AI never does alone. For anything that touches personal data, money, hiring, legal text or customers, those rules matter more than which model you pick.

Watch for work that only moves desks. If the model saves a support agent five minutes but the team lead now spends ten checking drafts, the chore just changed owners. Count the whole loop, review time included, before you call it a win.

Start with one chore and a human gate

Anthropic's engineering team has a rule for building with LLMs that fits office workflows too: find the simplest solution possible and add complexity only when it clearly improves the outcome (Building effective agents, December 2024). In practice:

  • Pick one chore that happens at least weekly and has a clear owner.
  • Write down the input, the output and what "good" looks like, with two or three real examples.
  • Let the model write the first draft. A person reviews every output before it goes anywhere.
  • Run it for two or three weeks. Note the time saved, the time spent reviewing and the cases it got wrong.
  • Keep it, tweak it or drop it. Dropping it is a perfectly good result.

If you want the build side in more detail, Small AI Workflows That Actually Save You Hours walks through turning a chore into a saved workflow. If the gate feels fuzzy, Using AI Without Handing Over Your Judgment looks at where that line belongs.

There's a nice side effect. Once you start looking, you also find chores nobody needs. Why does every release start from a blank checklist? Why does the weekly report need copy-paste from four tools? Sometimes the best fix is a template, a small script or deleting the report. That still counts, and you found it because you went looking.

Try this week

  • Keep a friction log for five working days. Every time you think "this shouldn't take this long", write one line.
  • Pick the item that repeats most and split it into reading steps and deciding steps.
  • Run the reading steps through a model with three real inputs and compare the output with what you'd have done.
  • If it holds up, run it for two weeks with a person reviewing every output, and count the review time too.

faqs.q: Where should a team look for its first AI use case?
faqs.a: Look at chores that repeat at least weekly and are mostly reading, gathering, matching, reformatting or drafting: onboarding material, support answers, reconciliation, meeting prep. Let the model take that first pass and keep a person on the decision. Starting there means nobody has to trust the model with a call on day one.

faqs.q: What is the jagged technological frontier?
faqs.a: It's the name Dell'Acqua and colleagues gave to an uneven edge in AI ability. In their 2023 experiment with 758 BCG consultants, GPT-4 users did more work, faster and at higher quality on tasks inside the model's ability, but were 19 percentage points less likely to get a correct answer on a task outside it. Tasks that look equally hard to people can land on different sides of that edge.

faqs.q: Does AI help every worker equally?
faqs.a: Not in the studies so far. In the NBER study of 5,179 customer support agents, issues resolved per hour rose 14% on average and 34% for novice and low-skilled agents, with minimal impact on experienced, highly skilled agents. Results from one job and one tool won't transfer directly to yours, so test in your own work.

faqs.q: How do I know if an AI pilot actually saved time?
faqs.a: Measure the whole loop for two or three weeks: time saved on the task, time spent reviewing the output and the cases it got wrong. If review time eats the savings, the work only moved to someone else's desk. Keeping, tweaking or dropping the pilot are all fine outcomes.
